newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE-Romanian-born girl, 10, is painter to the stars.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Romanian-born girl, 10, is painter to the stars.

text.p: She is called urechila or "big ears" in her native Romanian because "I see everything and I hear everything," a nickname she much prefers to "the pint-sized Picasso" given in her press clippings.
Alexandra Nechita, 10 years old and less than 5 feet (1.5 metres) tall, has not yet entered the sixth grade but has already sold several of her colourful abstract canvases for $50,000 apiece.

A prodigy in the mould of Mozart, according to some of the publicity swirling about her, she has appeared on U.S. network television and in national publications. Her unschooled works have been purchased by the likes of rock stars Melissa Etheridge and Paul Stanley, actress Ellen Degeneres and various collectors. Museum curators are giving her advice about her output.

The charming and precocious Nechita, who fled with her mother from her native Romania when she was two, was in Chicago recently to promote yet another exhibition. She has seemingly remained unaffected and unspoiled by the attention.

"I don't remember anything from when I was born because I was very very tiny but I went back (to Romania) twice," she said in her lightly accented English. "When I went back the second time, at the airport there were hundreds and hundreds of reporters and cameras. I said, 'Mommy, the president came back,' because the first time I was there he was gone. Then the first thing I knew they were asking me questions and I thought, 'Oh, my gosh!'"

Nechita submitted to roughly 300 press interviews during her spring European tour but managed to squeeze in visits to art museums and see the works of earlier artists. "I like Picasso, I like Matisse, Miro, Chagall, Modigliani, Kandinsky, Klee, Braque," she said, counting off on her fingers. "I just started to read a history of Picasso."

Her auburn hair in neat plaits and her child's frame draped in an oversized jean jacket over a white T-shirt and red jean skirt, she curled up on a gallery office couch clutching an oversized pillow and answered questions about her young life. She said she loves classical music, especially Vivaldi, which she listens to while painting in the afternoons after school and on weekends. And she insisted she is an otherwise "normal" schoolgirl who enjoys sports, rollerblading and watching cartoons on television.

Inspired by a trip to Disneyland and the Matterhorn thrill ride, Nechita returned to her Los Angeles studio and painted "Breathless," which features an upended figure stretched around the canvas, with blotches and swirls of colour. Another painting, "Summer in Europe," depicts an angular Nechita with an extra set of eyes, reminiscent of the early 20th century cubists to which her work has been compared. But she said the eyes are merely indicative of her highly tuned senses.

Her artistic gifts have purposely not been refined in art schools, following the advice of a former teacher. She has never made a figurative drawing and does not plan to attend art school until her teenage years.

"I started painting without knowing anything about Picasso, without knowing about Braque, Miro. It was all something from inside me. It was a motivation I had inside me. After I had my first exhibition, a few weeks or so later I went to Los Angeles County Museum and saw my first paintings by Picasso. That was a very big encouragement for me, (but) I still painted the same way, in the same style," she said.

"Then when I sold my first painting for $50, that was a very very big surprise for me. It was my first exhibit and I didn't think anybody would appreciate my artwork. Some people were doubtful, you know -- 'She's just an eight-year-old, big deal, any eight-year-old can do this.' It was my fifth or sixth exhibit when Ben (agent Ben Valenty) had discovered me, and that's when prices went higher and everything changed -- a lot."

Nechita said she will continue painting in her paint-spattered "magic slippers" no matter what happens to her meteoric career. "I might do some etching, I might sculpt, I might do some ceramics, but I'll still paint."
